extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer, which is either "yes" or "no".
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. 2019. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was gathered using the pipeline from Natural Questions with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word was in a manually constructed set of indicator words and that were of sufficient length. Questions were kept only if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results, after which the question and Wikipedia page were given to a human annotator. Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: deciding whether the question was good (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information), finding a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question or marking it not answerable, and finally marking whether the answer was yes or no. The final dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set, for a total of 16k questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators could mark questions as "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries and Wikipedia pages returned among the first five search results. The dataset also includes an additional 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Unlike in Natural Questions, the authors only used questions marked as having a yes/no answer, and paired each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document. They combined 13k questions from their pipeline with 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set, then split the data into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from Natural Questions were always in the train set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word was in a manually constructed set of indicator words and that were of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. Questions were further filtered to those marked as good, answerable from the article, and having a yes/no answer. The final examples use the selected passage rather than the full document to reduce ambiguity and keep inputs small enough for existing entailment models.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotators labeled question/article pairs in three steps. First, before seeing the Wikipedia page, they judged whether the question was good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information. Second, for good questions, they found a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question, or marked the question as not answerable if the article did not contain the requested information. Third, they marked whether the answer was yes or no. For annotation quality assessment, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples; when they disagreed, they conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess annotation quality, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels. On these 110 examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the authors used singly annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples for quality assessment.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that naturally occurring yes/no questions are directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions and have the benefit of being challenging while coming from natural sources rather than artificial settings. It also notes that engineered datasets risk producing models optimized for artificial settings without obvious end-use applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is slightly class imbalanced, with yes answers more common (62.31% in the train set). The paper also notes correlations between question topic or type and the likelihood of a yes answer, though these are too weak to outperform the majority baseline. Passage-only models perform above the majority baseline, suggesting some language patterns in passages correlate with the answer.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset uses singly annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets. Annotation errors included ambiguous or debatable cases and cases where annotators misunderstood the passage. The paper notes that the analysis of reasoning categories may be slightly out of date because the dataset was updated after that analysis. The current dataset pairs questions with selected passages rather than full documents; the authors suggest a document-level version would be more difficult and closer to an end-user application.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a reading comprehension benchmark for answering naturally occurring yes/no questions and for studying inference in natural language understanding. The paper defines train, dev, and test splits of 9.4k, 3.2k, and 3.2k examples respectively, and uses the dataset for training, fine-tuning, development, and testing of yes/no QA models.
